{{Short description|Model of information available at a given point of a random process}}
In the [[stochastic process|theory of stochastic processes]], a subdiscipline of [[probability theory]], '''filtrations''' are [[Total order|totally ordered]] collections of subsets that are used to model the information that is available at a given point and therefore play an important role in the formalization of random (stochastic) processes.

== Definition ==
Let <math> (\Omega, \mathcal A, P) </math> be a [[probability space]] and let <math> I </math> be an [[index set]] with a [[total order]] <math> \leq </math> (often <math> \N </math>,  <math> \R^+ </math>, or a subset of <math> \mathbb R^+ </math>).

For every <math> i \in I </math> let <math> \mathcal F_i </math> be a [[Sigma-algebra#Sub σ-algebras|sub-''σ''-algebra]] of <math> \mathcal A </math>. Then
:<math> \mathbb F:= (\mathcal F_i)_{i \in I} </math>

is called a filtration, if <math> \mathcal F_k \subseteq \mathcal F_\ell</math> for all <math> k \leq \ell </math>. So filtrations are families of ''σ''-algebras that are ordered non-decreasingly.<ref name="Klenke191" /> If <math> \mathbb F </math> is a filtration, then  <math> (\Omega, \mathcal A, \mathbb F, P) </math> is called a '''filtered probability space'''.

== Example ==
Let <math> (X_n)_{n \in \N} </math> be a [[stochastic process]] on the probability space <math>  (\Omega, \mathcal A, P)  </math>. 
Let <math> \sigma(X_k  \mid k \leq n) </math> denote the [[Σ-algebra#σ-algebra_generated_by_random_variable_or_vector| ''σ''-algebra generated by the random variables]] <math> X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n </math>.
Then 
:<math> \mathcal F_n:=\sigma(X_k \mid k \leq n) </math>

is a ''σ''-algebra and  <math> \mathbb F= (\mathcal F_n)_{n \in \N} </math> is a filtration.

<math> \mathbb F </math> really is a filtration, since by definition all <math> \mathcal F_n </math> are ''σ''-algebras and
:<math> \sigma(X_k \mid k \leq n) \subseteq \sigma(X_k \mid k \leq n+1). </math>
This is known as the [[natural filtration]] of <math>\mathcal A</math> with respect to <math>(X_n)_{n \in \N}</math>.

== Types of filtrations ==
=== Right-continuous filtration ===
If <math> \mathbb F= (\mathcal F_i)_{i \in I} </math> is a filtration, then the corresponding '''right-continuous filtration''' is defined as<ref name="Kallenberg350" />
:<math> \mathbb F^+:= (\mathcal F_i^+)_{i \in I}, </math>

with
:<math> \mathcal F_i^+:= \bigcap_{z > i} \mathcal F_z. </math>
The filtration <math> \mathbb F </math> itself is called right-continuous if <math> \mathbb F^+ = \mathbb F </math>.<ref name="Klenke462" />

=== Complete filtration ===
Let <math> (\Omega, \mathcal F, P) </math> be a probability space, and let
:<math> \mathcal N_P:= \{A \subseteq \Omega \mid A \subseteq B \text{ for some } B \in  \mathcal F \text{ with } P(B)=0 \} </math>
be the set of all sets that are contained within a <math> P </math>-[[null set]].

A filtration <math> \mathbb F= (\mathcal F_i)_{i \in I} </math> is called a '''complete filtration''', if every <math> \mathcal F_i </math> contains <math> \mathcal N_P </math>. This implies <math> (\Omega, \mathcal F_i, P) </math> is a [[complete measure space]] for every <math> i \in I. </math> (The converse is not necessarily true.)

=== Augmented filtration ===
A filtration is called an '''augmented filtration''' if it is complete and right continuous. For every filtration <math> \mathbb F </math> there exists a smallest augmented filtration <math> \tilde {\mathbb F} </math> refining <math> \mathbb F </math>.

If a filtration is an augmented filtration, it is said to satisfy the '''usual hypotheses''' or the '''usual conditions'''.<ref name="Klenke462" />
